title: Metrics Monitoring
prompt: Design a metrics ingestion, storage, and querying system like Prometheus or Datadog. The system must collect time-series metrics (CPU, memory, request latency) from thousands of hosts, store them durably, and support real-time alerting and historical queries. Target ~1M samples/sec ingest, 99.9% availability, sub-second query latency on recent data, and 1-year retention with tiered storage.

stages.title: Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core functional requirements?
stages.howToAnswer: Ingest metrics from agents, store time-series data, query with filters/aggregations, define alerts. Don't drift into visualization (Grafana) or advanced ML features.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Stock Price Ticker):
bullets: Agents push stock prices (AAPL, GOOG) at regular intervals
Query: 'Get average AAPL price over the last hour'
Alert: 'Notify if AAPL drops below threshold'

must: Accept metrics (name, timestamp, value, labels) from multiple agents
Store metrics durably and retrieve them by name, labels, and time range
Query metrics with aggregations (sum, avg, max) and label filters
Evaluate alert rules and forward to notification system
should: Support sampling / downsampling for older data
Scrape or pull metrics automatically via service discovery
avoid: Designing the alerting notification UI — that's handled downstream
Confusing metrics (time-series) with logs or traces

stages.sampleAnswer:
1. Agents (via scrape or push) send metrics: name, timestamp, numeric value, key-value labels.
2. Store raw metrics in a time-series database, partitioned by series ID.
3. Query API: retrieve samples by metric name, label filters, and time range; apply aggregation (sum, avg, max, min).
4. Alert engine: evaluate rule expressions on incoming/recent samples; fire alerts matching a threshold.
5. Optionally: downsample old data to coarser intervals to save space.
hints: Think of a metric as a labeled numeric stream over time. What's the minimal data you need to capture it?
Two separate operations: storing raw samples vs. aggregating them. Keep them distinct.
Alerts aren't dashboards — they're a rules engine that watches for conditions and fires.

stages.title: Non-Functional Requirements
stages.howToAnswer: Ingest rate, query latency, retention, availability, durability. Put numbers on everything.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Stock Price Ticker):
bullets: Query latency: <500ms for 1-hour window, <5s for 1-year window

must: Ingest throughput (samples/sec)
Query latency targets for recent vs. historical data
Data retention period and storage scale
Durability: no sample loss on single-host failure
should: Alert delivery latency (e.g., <1 min to detection)
avoid: Ignoring the write-heavy, read-sparse nature of time-series systems
Forgetting that old data must be queried cheaply (not sacrificing P99)

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Ingest: 1M samples/sec sustained (1K hosts × 1K metrics/host, or 10K hosts × 100 metrics/host).
- Cardinality: up to 1B unique series (hostname × metric × labels).
- Query latency: <1s for recent data (last 24h), <5s for monthly aggregations.
- Retention: 1 year raw data; older data downsampled to 1h intervals.
- Durability: no sample loss; multi-AZ replication for storage.
- Availability: 99.9% uptime; queries degrade gracefully on partial outage.
- Alert detection: <1 min from sample ingestion to alert firing.
hints: Cardinality (number of unique label combinations) often dominates cost. What constraint helps you bound it?
Recent queries (last 24h) are hot. Old queries are rare. Tier your storage accordingly.
Ingest is write-heavy. Don't use a schema that forces index writes on every sample.

stages.title: Core Entities
stages.howToAnswer: Metric (the stream), Sample (a single data point), Series (metric + label set), Alert Rule.

must: Sample: (timestamp, value) — the atomic unit
Series: (metric name, label set) — identifies a unique stream
AlertRule: expression, threshold, evaluation window
should: Chunk: a compressed block of samples
avoid: Treating samples and series as the same thing

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Sample: { timestamp (Unix ns or ms), value (float64) }.
- Series: { metric_name (string), labels (map<key, value>) }. Together, metric + labels form the unique series ID.
- SeriesMetadata: { seriesID, lastUpdatedAt, chunkRefs }.
- Chunk: a compressed block of (timestamp, value) pairs, typically 2-4h of data per chunk.
- AlertRule: { name, expr (PromQL-like), for (evaluation window), severity, action (notification target) }.
hints: A series is uniquely identified by metric name + label set. How do you assign it a stable ID?
Chunks are immutable once written. Why does this matter for concurrent ingest?
Labels are sparse — most series won't have all possible label keys. What data structure handles this?

stages.title: API
stages.howToAnswer: Scrape targets via pull, query with filters/aggregation, define rules. Keep it minimal — internal components talk via efficient protocols.

exampleHints.headline: Example (Stock Price Ticker):
bullets: GET /metrics → returns all symbol prices in Prometheus format
POST /api/query body: { query: 'avg(stock_price) by (symbol)', start, end }
POST /api/rules body: { expr, threshold, for, action }

must: Scrape endpoint (pull-based metrics collection)
Query endpoint (time range, filters, aggregations)
Alert rule definition and status endpoint
avoid: Inventing complex push APIs — pull is simpler at scale

stages.sampleAnswer:
Pull (Scrape):
GET /metrics
  → Prometheus-format output:
    http_requests_total{method="GET",path="/api",status="200"} 1234
    cpu_usage_percent{host="node1"} 45.2

Query:
POST /api/query
  body: { query: "avg(cpu_usage_percent) by (host)", start: 1000000, end: 2000000, step: 60 }
  → { data: [ { labels: {host: "node1"}, values: [[ts1, 45.2], [ts2, 44.8], ...] }, ... ] }

Alerts:
GET /api/rules → list all alert rules
POST /api/rules body: { name, expr, for_sec, severity }
GET /api/alerts → list currently firing alerts
hints: Scrape format is simple — agent outputs key=value pairs. How do you parse and normalize it?
Query needs a time-series query language (or simple filters). What's the minimal query surface?
Alert rules live in Prometheus. How do they flow to the external Alertmanager?

stages.title: High-Level Design
stages.questionPrompt: Sketch the architecture. Walk through the ingest and query paths.
stages.howToAnswer: Service discovery → scrape pool → ingester → TSDB storage. Query router → TSDB read layer → Alertmanager. Highlight the headline trick: pull-based scrape with series partitioning, chunk compression, and separate hot/cold storage.

must: Service discovery component (Consul, Kubernetes API, static config)
Stateless scraper pool that pulls metrics from targets
Ingester that buffers and writes to TSDB
TSDB storage partitioned by series ID (e.g., hash(metric+labels) % shards)
Chunk compression (delta encoding, bitpacking)
Query router that hits recent hot data and tiered cold storage
Alert rule evaluator and dedup before fan-out to Alertmanager
should: Bloom filter or inverted index for label lookups
Write-Ahead Log (WAL) for durability between flushes
Background compaction of chunks and blocks
avoid: Treating all samples equally — tier by age
Push-only ingest — pull gives you better control

stages.sampleAnswer:
Ingest Path:
1. Service Discovery: reads Consul/K8s API every 30s. Builds a dynamic list of scrape targets (host, port, labels).
2. Scraper Pool: N stateless scraper pods, each responsible for a hash-based subset of targets. Pulls /metrics from each target every 15s (configurable). Parses Prometheus format.
3. Ingester: batches samples in memory (buffer 2-3 min of data). Assigns each unique (metric, labels) pair to a series ID via a sharded series-ID allocator (Cassandra or DynamoDB). Writes (timestamp, value) to a local Chunk in memory.
4. TSDB Blocks: every 2 hours, the ingester flushes accumulated chunks to disk as an immutable Block. Block contains index (series → chunks), compressed chunks, and metadata.
5. WAL: samples are write-ahead-logged before buffering in memory, so a crash replays uncommitted data.
6. Tiered Storage: recent blocks (< 24h) kept in fast SSD; older blocks moved to S3/GCS (cold storage).

Query Path:
1. Query hits a stateless Query Service (load-balanced).
2. Label lookup: for a query like 'cpu_usage{host="node1"}', use the label index to find matching series IDs.
3. Chunk lookup: once we have series IDs, find which blocks contain samples in the requested time range.
4. Hot-path (recent data): read from in-memory Ingester or fast SSD blocks. Merge results.
5. Cold-path (old data): read downsampled blocks from S3. Downsampling reduces query cost (1h samples instead of 1m).
6. Aggregation: apply PromQL operations (sum, avg, rate) on the merged samples.

Alert Path:
1. Alert Rule Evaluator: every 15s (configurable), read each rule. Execute the query expression against the TSDB.
2. Thresholding: if the result crosses the threshold, mark the alert as FIRING. If below for 'for' window, mark RESOLVED.
3. Dedup: multiple Prometheus replicas may independently fire the same alert. A dedup layer (Redis or in-memory state) groups identical alerts by (rule, labels) and only forwards one copy to Alertmanager.
4. Fan-out to Alertmanager: send firing alerts. Alertmanager handles grouping, routing, and delivery (email, Slack, PagerDuty).
hints: The headline trick: partition scrape targets by hash so one scraper always owns the same target. Why does this help?
Chunk compression is critical: delta encoding + bitpacking can reduce 1-year data to petabytes instead of exabytes. Understand the encoding.
Tiered storage: recent queries hit memory/SSD. Old queries hit downsampled blocks. How does downsampling work (e.g., keep only hourly max/min/avg)?

dataFlow.title: Data Flow
dataFlow.description: Metrics flow from agents through scraping, buffering, compression, and multi-tier storage, with queries routed to hot or cold tiers and alerts evaluated and deduplicated before fan-out.

deepDives.title: Cardinality explosion
deepDives.questionPrompt: Your cardinality grows to 10B series. TSDB explodes in memory and query time becomes unbounded. How do you detect and mitigate runaway cardinality without losing data?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Prevention: enforce cardinality limits per metric (e.g., max 1M unique series per metric). If a label (like user_id or request_id) has unbounded values, drop it from ingestion or replace it with a hash bucket. Detection: track the cardinality of each metric in a side-car process; if it exceeds a threshold, alert ops. Mitigation: 1) relabel rules to drop high-cardinality labels before writing, 2) rate-limit ingest on problematic metrics, 3) evict old series more aggressively. Storage: store cardinality estimates (HyperLogLog) per metric to enable quick queries without materializing all series.

must: Cardinality limit per metric with concrete action on breach (drop, rate-limit, relabel)
Detection mechanism (monitoring cardinality growth)
should: Relabel rules to drop high-cardinality dimensions
HyperLogLog or similar for cheap cardinality estimation
avoid: Storing all series in memory without bounds

hints: If a label has unbounded values (like timestamps or IDs), it's a cardinality bomb. How do you detect it before it crashes the system?
Relabel rules let you drop or rename labels at scrape time. Why is this better than post-hoc deletion?
Cardinality is hard to query directly — use a probabilistic data structure.

deepDives.title: Out-of-order samples and consistency
deepDives.questionPrompt: Samples arrive out-of-order (slow scraper, network jitter). How do you handle them without dropping data or breaking time-series continuity? And how do you ensure query results are consistent even during partial failures?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Out-of-order: accept samples with timestamps up to T-max_drift (e.g., 24h old) using a rolling time window. Store them in a separate 'ooo' buffer and merge with the main chunk on flush. This avoids breaking the immutability of committed chunks. Consistency: on multi-replica systems (e.g., Prometheus HA pairs), deduplicate and pick the highest timestamp if there's a conflict. For queries, snapshot the WAL and block list at query start time — don't allow queries to race the ingest path. Eventually-consistent is OK because time-series are append-only.

must: Mechanism to accept out-of-order samples (buffer or rolling window)
Merge strategy when flushing (preserve all, dedup on higher timestamp)
should: Snapshot isolation (queries see a consistent view)

hints: Out-of-order samples will always happen in production (GC pauses, network jitter). What's the acceptable window?
Chunks are immutable once flushed. Where do out-of-order samples live before being merged?
Multi-replica dedup: if two Prometheus servers scrape the same target and you see conflicting values, which one do you keep?

deepDives.title: Alert evaluation and dedup at scale
deepDives.questionPrompt: You have 10K alert rules and 1M samples/sec. Evaluating every rule every 15s is expensive. How do you scale rule evaluation? And how do you deduplicate alerts from multiple Prometheus replicas before notifying?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Scaling rule evaluation: partition rules by hash across multiple evaluation workers (similar to scraper sharding). Each worker is responsible for a subset of rules and evaluates them concurrently. Cache query results across rules that share the same expression (e.g., multiple rules querying 'rate(http_errors_total)'). Use an in-memory query result cache with a short TTL. Dedup: collect all firing alerts (rule name, label set) into a shared dedup state (Redis with a 10-min sliding window). If the same (rule, labels) pair fires from multiple replicas within a short window, deduplicate and send only one copy to Alertmanager. Alertmanager itself also groups and silences, so dedup is a first-pass filter.

must: Partition rule evaluation across workers (concrete: hash(rule_name) % num_workers)
Dedup mechanism with concrete state store (Redis, shared cache)
should: Query result caching within the evaluation window
avoid: Evaluating all rules on all replicas (N² cost)
Dedup delay > 10 min (users see duplicate notifications)

hints: Rule evaluation is CPU-bound. Partition rules like you partition scrape targets — what's the partitioning key?
Query result caching: two rules that both query the same expression should share the cached result. How long should you cache it?
Dedup window: if a rule fires on two replicas at t=0 and t=2s, should you send one alert or two?
